ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, it is known that in $\triangle ABC$, $\angle C=60^\circ$, BD bisects $\angle ABC$, and AD bisects the external angle $\angle CAE$. What is the degree measure of $\angle D$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Since BD bisects $\angle ABC$ and AD bisects the exterior angle $\angle CAE$,\\
it follows that $\angle DBA= \frac{1}{2}\angle ABC$ and $\angle DAE= \frac{1}{2}\angle CAE$,\\
Given that $\angle CAE=\angle ABC+\angle C$,\\
and $\angle DAE=\angle ABD+\angle D$,\\
it can be derived that $\angle D= \frac{1}{2}\angle CAE- \frac{1}{2} \angle ABD= \frac{1}{2} (\angle CAE-\angle ABD)= \frac{1}{2} \angle C=\frac{1}{2}\times 60^\circ=\boxed{30^\circ}$;

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the three points E, A, and B are on the same straight line, A is at the lower left, B is at the lower right, C is above, and D is at the upper left. The line segments AC, BC, AD, and BD are all drawn, and the angle to be found is the angle formed by AD and BD at point D. Then reason: Let ∠ABC = x. Because BD bisects ∠ABC, ∠ABD = x/2. Also because AE is the extension line of AB, ∠CAE is the exterior angle of △ABC at point A, therefore ∠CAE = ∠ABC + ∠C = x + 60°. AD bisects the exterior angle ∠CAE, so ∠DAE = (x + 60°)/2. Since A, E, and B are collinear, ∠DAB = 180° - ∠DAE = 180° - (x + 60°)/2. In △ADB, ∠ADB = 180° - ∠ABD - ∠DAB = 180° - x/2 - [180° - (x + 60°)/2] = 30°. Therefore ∠D = ∠ADB = 30°.
